brief.head: Museum homework
brief.text: Before each museum in Spain, Amit Varma asked ChatGPT Deep Research for an art-history lesson. Soon he could roughly guess the year of a Velázquez painting. {097-S01}

brief.head: Why context counts
brief.text: Nomsita asked whether art should not stand on its own. It should, Amit Varma said, but the artist’s journey and the ferment of the times deepen appreciation. {097-C03}

brief.head: The prolific privilege
brief.text: Pablo Picasso may have painted more than any painter ever, Amit Varma said, because success let him keep going. Unsuccessful painters eventually quit for something else. {097-C13}

brief.head: Genius at Starbucks
brief.text: Picasso’s café circle in Paris, Amit Varma said, was like the greatest minds of the age gathering at your local BKC Starbucks, unrecognised until much later. {097-J09}

brief.head: A page a day
brief.text: Amit Varma’s first must-read is EH Gombrich’s *The Story of Art*, which goes painting by painting. Read a page a day, he said, and it will expand your brain. {097-R21}

thought.text: It takes a long time to grow young.
thought.who: Pablo Picasso, quoted by Amit Varma as a philosophy of ageing

lead.kicker: Amit Varma’s Spanish holiday, and what it taught him
lead.head: Old masters, new tricks
body: Amit Varma spent fifteen days in Spain, walking about eight kilometres a day and giving himself an education in art. He came home with a thesis about old age.

He had looked hardest at five Spanish painters: Diego Velázquez, Francisco Goya, Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró and Salvador Dali. All were national icons by their thirties, yet the work that spoke to him most came in their fifties to eighties.

“All five of them, in my opinion, did their greatest work when they were really old, when they had no need to even try new things,” Varma told Ajay Shah. “But they kept reinventing themselves.” {097-C01}
Most people who reach such a peak, he said, coast on their past glories and rarely rock the boat for fear of losing their fans.
Varma set this against the myth of youthful genius: Kurt Cobain’s line that it is better to burn out than to fade away, and the rock musicians who died at 27.
At 21, Varma admitted, he fantasised about dying at 27 after achieving something great. “I achieved nothing great, so I postponed it.” {097-J01}
Shah and Susan had planned to do cool things by 29 and then give up. Then 29 came along, and, Shah said, “we settled into a marathon.”
## Craft first, art later
A teenage guitar prodigy can play Eddie Van Halen licks perfectly, Varma said. The craft is all there. “Does the art come now? The art doesn’t quite come now.” {097-C02}
Varma linked the art to thehraav, a settledness that comes with age.

Velázquez painted *Las Meninas* at 57. Goya, deaf and in his late seventies, covered the walls of his house with dark murals and told no one. Picasso, at 75, painted 58 versions of *Las Meninas*. Miró, in his eighties, said he was painting for the young of the future.
Goya, painting for no one, moved Varma almost as much by that freedom as by the work itself.
## Never too late
Varma read out Picasso’s line that one starts to get young at sixty, “and then it’s too late”. With longer lifespans, he told the 59-year-old Shah, it no longer is.

His message was for the 45-year-old stuck in a banking job who thinks he could have been a writer or a musician. “Could is not the word, can is the word,” Varma said. “It is never too late.” {097-C14}
This was no disdain for youth, he added, though he doubted Wim Wenders could have made *Perfect Days* in his thirties.
## The economist’s view

In finite fields such as chess, mathematics and theoretical physics, Shah said, people peak in their twenties to forties; economists peak in their forties to sixties. “The peak time for a CEO is the fifties. The perfect age for a founder in a startup is fifty,” he said. {097-C15} Fifty years of evidence show all these ages rising.
Longer healthspans are one reason, Shah said. Another is a research machine of PhDs, journals and grants that sets people free ever later.
What older minds do best, he argued, is integration: seeing the big picture across many perspectives, while the young write sharp, clean, cute code.
Varma turned the thesis on his co-host: that wisdom, he said, could not have come from the twenty-year-old Ajay Shah. Shah agreed: “Absolutely.”
By then the light had gone. “I don’t even know if I’m visible anymore,” Varma said.

second.label: Bob Dylan at 56
second.head: Elvis would have to wait
second.deck: A brush with death, survived, gave Amit Varma his favourite Dylan album
body: At 56, Bob Dylan was in hospital with pericarditis and thought he was going to die. {097-S09} He even gave a quote, as Amit Varma told it: “I think I’m going to see Elvis soon.” {097-J14}

He survived, and that year made *Time Out of Mind*, Varma’s favourite Dylan album. Its song *Not Dark Yet* has the lines: “Sometimes my burden is more than I can bear. It’s not dark yet, but it’s getting there.” {097-R14}

It is a period, Varma noted, that the Dylan biopic won’t show. He raised it just after recalling how fans branded Dylan a Judas for going electric: they had come for the photograph Dylan left of himself, not the man.

quote.text: Dylan writes this when he’s in hospital earlier that year with pericarditis, and he thinks he’s going to die.

second.caption: Dylan’s brush with death

third.head: Too real for the Pope
body: A court painter was expected to flatter his patrons, Amit Varma said. Diego Velázquez kept going a little beyond that.
Court tradition painted the royal buffoons and dwarfs as caricatures. Velázquez painted one dwarf as a learned, thoughtful man.

In 1650, at 51, he painted Pope Innocent the Fifth, if Varma remembered correctly. The Pope hated it, because it was too real. {097-S03} “A painter is not just picking up what he sees in front of him,” Varma said, “but also telling a deeper truth that he might be able to perceive.”
He painted the writers Aesop and Menippus as beggars, and Varma has stood before both at the Prado. {#aesop} By then, Varma said, “he’s not hinting at depths. He’s actually telling you stories.”
third.caption: the Pope’s unflattering portrait

p2.title: Busy being born
p2.deck: Four Spanish painters who kept reinventing themselves, in Amit Varma’s telling, with a coda from Ajay Shah {097-J04}

sections.label: The first master
sections.head: Only you shall paint me
sections.caption: Velázquez and Las Meninas
body: Diego Velázquez was born in 1599, Amit Varma said, into a world with no cinema, few books and no way of seeing most of the art made before him. {#velazquez}

His teacher, Pacheco, was a mediocre realist who trained him in the classics. Yet at 19 Velázquez painted *Old Woman Frying Eggs*, and at 20 *The Waterseller of Seville*, hinting at depths beyond what was in front of him.
There was no art market, only royal patronage. In 1624, at about 25, he was summoned by King Philip IV, who loved his portrait and decreed that only Velázquez would paint him. {097-S02}
He kept seeking influences: time with Rubens in 1628, then a year and a half in Italy from 1629.
## A canvas to walk into
*Las Meninas*, painted in 1656 when he was 57, is his most powerful work. Standing before it, Varma felt he could walk into it. {097-S04}

There is an open door at the back, light from the right, and a distant mirror holding the royal couple, who may be standing where we are. Velázquez painted himself at work. It is, Varma said, “much more enigmatic than that famous enigmatic Mona Lisa”. {097-J06}
Goya called Velázquez the only artist worth imitating, and Picasso sat at the Prado copying both. {#prado}
~ For Varma it was the first sign of his thesis: technique had become second nature, and “there he is now playing at another level”.

quote.text: Not exclusively mine, as in you’re only going to paint me, but only you are going to paint me. I am exclusively yours

sections.label: The second master
sections.head: Deaf ears, open eyes
sections.caption: Goya’s deafness and dark satire
body: Francisco Goya became a court painter young, Amit Varma said, like his hero Velázquez. Then, at 47, he went deaf. {#goyadeaf}

By 1797 or 1798 he had produced *Los Caprichos*, satirical etchings drawn, in Goya’s words, from “the multitudes of faults and vices common in every civil society”. *He Broke the Jug* shows children being beaten. Perhaps Varma’s favourite is *The Dream of Reason Produces Monsters*, which Goya meant as the cover.
In 1800 Charles IV commissioned a family portrait. Goya made the royals look like “weird people with their own internal dramas”, and painted himself painting them, a nod to *Las Meninas*.
## Stolen, then owned

His 1808 execution scene, with faceless French soldiers and a lantern lighting the man in the white shirt, resurfaces in Picasso’s *Guernica* and *Massacre in Korea*. Critics dislike the latter; Varma calls it a masterpiece. {097-R07}
Varma saw in it the truth of Picasso’s maxim that good artists borrow and great artists steal. Stealing is not dishonourable, he said: it means making something completely your own. {097-C04}

~ Ajay Shah recalled John Maynard Keynes calling Newton not just the first of the scientists but the last of the magicians. Varma saw Goya the same way: the last of the old masters and the first of the moderns, a bridge between worlds like Istanbul. {097-C05}

quote.text: To steal in terms of art is to make something your own.

sections.label: The third master
sections.head: The long road to childhood
sections.caption: Picasso’s late playfulness
body: Pablo Picasso was mastering classical painting at 15 and 16, Amit Varma said, and would be a legend had he died after Cubism. What moved Varma most was what came later.
He read Picasso’s late sayings as a philosophy of ageing. You master technique young, then spend a lifetime learning to drop it and play like a child. {097-C07}
Picasso called his work a way of keeping a diary, and said he was always doing what he could not yet do, in order to learn how.
## Prisoners of the hit
Varma compared it with music. Once a song becomes famous, he said, a musician is tied to it, and spends the rest of his life covering his younger self. {097-C09}
U2, in relatively old age, came out with a whole bunch of cover versions of their own songs. {#u2}

Picasso painted until he died in his late eighties, and much of it was shown only after his death. Varma had no patience for the critics who sneered at it. Of *Self Portrait Facing Death* he asked: “Is this not genius? Is this not masterful?” {097-R08}
~ Late bloomers, Varma joked, feed his Bengali procrastination: he can waste twenty more years, and do his best work at 70 or 80. {097-J13}

quote.text: When I was young I could draw like Rafael. But it has taken me a lifetime to draw like a child.
quote.who: Pablo Picasso, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: The fourth master
sections.head: A single line, years long
sections.caption: Miró’s stripped-down canvases
body: Joan Miró, Amit Varma said, wanted to get past the clichés of how things are depicted, towards the essential. He thought in terms of poetry and music.
A musician cannot explain why a set of notes makes you cry, and neither can you. “Sometimes we demand too much explanation from artists,” Varma said. {097-C11}
## Rooms of almost nothing
At the Fundació Joan Miró in Barcelona he stood in a room of large canvases that were a single line, or a single blotch of colour. *Blue I*, *II* and *III* were painted when Miró was 65. {#blue}
“It took me only a moment to draw this line with a brush,” Miró said of one, “but it took me months, perhaps even years of reflection to form the idea of it.” {097-C12}
Peers and critics said such work was easy to parody. In his eighties, Miró answered that he was painting not for them but for the young of the future. {097-S11}
~ His rule for staying alive as an artist, which Varma read out, was to always work against yourself and destroy your past accomplishments. {097-C10}

quote.text: I’m not painting for you guys. I’m painting for the young of the future. I want my work to inspire them.

sections.label: More late mastery
sections.head: Late starters, longer runs
sections.caption: late bloomers and the rising peak age
body: Some artists master their craft young and keep going; others start late, Amit Varma said. Penelope Fitzgerald wrote her first novel after 60. {097-R16}
His favourite of hers, *The Gate of Angels*, was written in her mid-seventies. {#gate}

Beethoven went deaf around the same time as Goya, and wrote his famous string quartets after ten years or more of deafness. “The din from outside is gone, but there is a din from inside,” Varma said. {097-S12}
## Two forces

Ajay Shah said peak ages differ by field, early in chess and later for startup founders, at about fifty, and that all have been rising. One force is good news: longer healthspans let people keep piling up knowledge across fields.

The other is bad news. Science has become a business of PhDs, publishing, journal editors and grants, and the age at which researchers win their first grant keeps rising. “At the point where a person first gets funded is really the point at which they get free,” Shah said. {097-C16}
His ideal is to give brilliant young people autonomy early, and long healthspans as well.
~ Older people, Shah argued, should change the nature of their work: from a young programmer’s cute code to seeing the big picture and integrating knowledge. {097-C17}

quote.text: One deep thing that comes as people get older is interdisciplinarity. You get to know many, many perspectives.

side.boxText: Madrid’s Prado runs from the Renaissance to Goya; the Reina Sofía holds modern art and a lot of Picasso; the Thyssen gives much of the twentieth century, pop art included. With context, Amit Varma said, it is a full education in art. {#museums}

contQuote.text: How can you be a hundred years before your time? Like you make so much possible by just doing that, by showing that it’s okay, you have permission to think in this way.

stories.caption: Goya’s Black Paintings
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the murals Goya painted for nobody
stories.head: What Goya kept to himself
body: Francisco Goya moved into a house called the Abode of the Deaf, Amit Varma said, after its previous owner, who was also deaf.

In his late seventies and grappling with mortality, he painted extremely dark murals on its walls. He never mentioned them to anyone. They were found after his death, and someone had the good sense to use a newly invented technique to lift them from the plaster.

They were not his only hidden work. *The Disasters of War*, etchings with titles like *Bury Them and Stay Silent*, went unseen for decades. They made Varma think of the Japanese artist Yoshihiro Tatsumi’s *The Push Man and Other Stories*. {097-R11}
Today the Black Paintings hang together in one room at the Prado: fourteen of them, though some say a fifteenth is somewhere in America. {#fourteen}
Varma spent half an hour there. He had almost left the building when he decided he wanted to go back. {097-R04}

The famous *Saturn Devouring His Son* moved him least, perhaps because he had seen it reproduced so often. His favourite is *The Dog*. Goya titled none of the paintings, and nothing about this one is explained. Is the mass at the bottom mud, or water? “Is it existential angst? We really don’t know what’s happening.”

~ Goya, Varma said, was decades ahead of everyone, anticipating the Impressionists and the Surrealists. What moved him almost as much was the secrecy. “He’s just doing it for the doing of them.” {097-S06}
stories.why: Goya made his darkest work for no audience at all. Free of any need for approval, the deaf old painter got decades ahead of his time, and the work became its own reason. {097-C06}
stories.postscript: Were it not for Picasso, Varma said, Goya might be his favourite painter of all time.

stories.caption: Picasso’s fifty-eight Las Meninas
stories.kicker: Amit Varma in a room at the Picasso Museum, Barcelona
stories.head: One painting, fifty-eight times
body: *Las Meninas* had devastated Pablo Picasso when he first saw it as a young man. In 1957, at 75, he went back to it and painted his own versions: 58 of them.

They hang in one room of the Picasso Museum in Barcelona, ordered by date. Large canvases are dated a day apart, and on one wall four were made on the same day. Amit Varma could not remember the exact dates, but the pace astonished him.
Varma watched a couple of visitors move past them at full speed in the opposite direction, not understanding what was going on. {097-S08}
~ Picasso was not trying to get it right, Varma said, “because there is no right”. Velázquez himself would have accepted that. {097-C08}
stories.why: One old master played with another’s late masterpiece. Picasso called his work a way of keeping a diary; seen in date order, the 58 canvases are a record of him growing day by day.

stories.start: There's a famous story about how something went wrong in a factory
stories.end: dollars for the seventy years in which I learned uh what to look for
stories.caption: Henry Ford’s seventy-year invoice
stories.kicker: A factory tale Amit Varma told to explain Miró
stories.head: Seventy years in a screwdriver
body: Something went wrong in a factory Henry Ford was running, Amit Varma said, and his best engineers could not fix it. So Ford called in the foremost man in the field, aged seventy or so.
The expert walked around, put his ear to something and did some tapping. Then he asked for a screwdriver, took out a bolt, moved something inside and put it back. Everything worked again.

Varma forgot the exact fee: “Let us say for now that it was eighty thousand dollars.” Ford asked for a breakdown. Item one was a dollar for changing the bolt. Item two was the rest, “for the seventy years in which I learned what to look for”. {097-S10}
~ Varma told it beside a line from Joan Miró: a stroke took a moment to draw, but years of reflection to conceive. {097-C12}
stories.why: Mastery is mostly invisible. The simple gesture of an old hand holds decades of judgement, and that judgement is what the invoice charged for. The same holds for a single line on a vast canvas.

stories.caption: Picasso’s leap into Cubism
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Picasso’s search for a new language
stories.head: Matisse checks the calendar
body: At 15 and 16, Pablo Picasso was already a master of classical painting. As a teenager in Barcelona he hung out at the café Els Quatre Gats, even designing its menu, before leaving for Paris.
In 1901 a close friend shot himself, and Picasso sank into his Blue Period; the Rose Period followed. Then he and his café circle tired of realism and every ism since.

African tribal art led Picasso to *Les Demoiselles d’Avignon*, around 1907. Henri Matisse, whom he admired, thought it a prank. Had Matisse owned a Garmin watch, Amit Varma joked, he would have checked whether it was April 1. {097-J07}
~ Braque saw what Picasso was doing, and the two built Cubism together without a hint of rivalry. {097-S07} They moved from analytic Cubism to synthetic.

quote.text: But there are other people who are like, yeah, boss, I see what you’re doing.

stories.postscript: After the First World War, Picasso turned back to neoclassicism: famous for Cubism, Varma said, but not tied to it.

quiz.q: Which tool did Amit Varma use to prepare for each museum he visited in Spain?
quiz.a: ChatGPT Deep Research, which wrote him a narrative art-history lesson for each.

quiz.q: Why did Pope Innocent hate the portrait Velázquez painted of him in 1650?
quiz.a: He said it was too real: Velázquez painted him as he saw him.

quiz.q: Where did Goya paint his Black Paintings, and who knew about them?
quiz.a: On the walls of his house; he told nobody, and they surfaced after his death.

quiz.q: What did Henri Matisse make of Picasso’s *Les Demoiselles d’Avignon* when he first saw it?
quiz.a: He thought it was a prank, a joke that could not possibly be serious.

quiz.q: At what age did Penelope Fitzgerald write her first novel, according to Amit Varma?
quiz.a: After sixty; *The Gate of Angels* came in her mid-seventies.

quiz.q: According to Ajay Shah, at what point does a young researcher really become free?
quiz.a: When they first get funded; otherwise they work in someone else’s lab.
